findings.claim: 35 of the 48 practice questions are labelled “20 marks — Extract Analysis”.
findings.truth: The 19th-century prose question is one source-based question worth 40 marks. All 35 relabelled “40 marks”; the other 13 already said 40.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md §2.2: ‘Section B (20%) 19th Century Prose (40 marks)… Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3.’

findings.claim: All 48 mark schemes carry invented ladders: 33 use 20-mark or 5-mark bands, 15 use an “AO1 (up to 10) … AO4 (up to 10)” split.
findings.truth: The board publishes no split of the 40 marks between objectives, and there is no AO4 on this question. All 48 rebuilt on the five house bands (33–40 / 25–32 / 17–24 / 9–16 / 1–8), keeping the top-band content and dropping the AO4 line.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md §2.2: ‘Section B (20%) 19th Century Prose (40 marks)… Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3.’

findings.claim: The board is named in student-facing text 18 times across all eight lessons — “the Eduqas exam”, “Eduqas Component 2 Section B”, and the spec code in “the Eduqas C720U exam” (lessons 1, 6, 7). Two lesson descriptions and two headings carry it.
findings.truth: House rule: Eduqas lessons never name the board or the spec code. Reworded to “the exam”, “your 19th-century prose question”, “this question”.
findings.evidence: House rule (Eduqas/WJEC neutral phrasing); CHECK_PROMPT banned-string list.

findings.claim: Lesson 8 states AO4 nine times as an objective the student is marked on: “The four Assessment Objectives”, “accurate expression (AO4) in every paragraph”, “Ignoring AO4 — sloppy expression loses marks”, “proofread for AO4 marks”, “address all four AOs”. Lessons 1 and 2 repeat it in their exam tips.
findings.truth: Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3 (context). Spelling, punctuation and grammar earn no marks on the 19th-century prose question — AO4 sits in Section A. All eleven places corrected to three objectives and a plain statement that SPaG carries no marks here.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md §2.2: ‘Section B (20%) 19th Century Prose (40 marks)… Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3.’

findings.claim: “The Eduqas question on A Christmas Carol is worth 40 marks, split equally across AO1, AO2, AO3, and AO4.”
findings.truth: The 40 marks are right; the equal split is invented and AO4 is not assessed here. Rewritten as “worth 40 marks and is marked on AO1, AO2 and AO3 (context)”.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md §2.2: ‘Section B (20%) 19th Century Prose (40 marks)… Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3.’

findings.claim: Knowledge check 2 asks “Which Assessment Objective tests your accuracy of written expression?” and keys AO4 as correct.
findings.truth: AO4 is not assessed on this question, so the item trains a wrong expectation. Retargeted to “Which Assessment Objective rewards your understanding of context?” with the key moved to AO3.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md §2.2: ‘Section B (20%) 19th Century Prose (40 marks)… Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3.’

findings.claim: Flashcard 12: “Why does the novella end at Christmas dinner?”
findings.truth: It does not. Scrooge goes to Fred’s dinner in the middle of Stave 5; the novella ends the next morning at the office with Bob Cratchit, then the closing narration. Reworded to ask how Stave 5 closes the circle with Fred.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/christmas-carol.txt Stave V: “But he was early at the office next morning… I am about to raise your salary!”

findings.claim: “The novella’s final line — ‘it was always said of him, that he knew how to keep Christmas well’”, repeated in flashcard 13 as “the novella’s closing line”.
findings.truth: The final line is “And so, as Tiny Tim observed, God bless Us, Every One!” The quoted phrase sits in the sentence before it. Changed to “the novella’s closing verdict on Scrooge” in both places.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/christmas-carol.txt last two sentences of Stave V.

findings.claim: Flashcard 8, defining allusion: “Marley’s chain alludes to biblical bondage.”
findings.truth: Unsupported. Dickens’s Stave 1 allusion is to Hamlet — the same point lesson 2’s own opening paragraph and lesson 1 both make. Answer changed to the Hamlet allusion.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/christmas-carol.txt Stave I: “If we were not perfectly convinced that Hamlet’s Father died before the play began…”

findings.claim: Flashcard 12 quotes Tiny Tim’s “empty seat in the corner”.
findings.truth: Dickens writes “I see a vacant seat… in the poor chimney-corner, and a crutch without an owner”. The card is a memorisation card, so the wording matters. Corrected to ‘vacant seat’.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/christmas-carol.txt Stave III, the Ghost’s reply about Tiny Tim.

findings.claim: “The ghost holds a glowing torch shaped like a ‘Horn of Plenty’” — given in quotation marks as Dickens’s wording.
findings.truth: Dickens writes “a glowing torch, in shape not unlike Plenty’s horn”. Corrected to ‘Plenty’s horn’.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/christmas-carol.txt Stave III, first description of the Ghost of Christmas Present.

findings.claim: The glossary pop-up attached to the word “metaphor” reads “An extended metaphor in which abstract ideas are represented through symbolic characters or events.”
findings.truth: That is the definition of allegory, and lesson 3’s own flashcard 11 uses the same sentence for ‘allegory’. A student tapping ‘metaphor’ gets the wrong term defined. Replaced with a definition of metaphor.
findings.evidence: Internal contradiction with lesson 3 flashcard 11 and lesson 4 glossary ‘allegory’.

findings.claim: “In 1843, Dickens read a Parliamentary Commission report on the employment of women and children in mines and factories.”
findings.truth: The report Dickens read in February 1843 was the Second Report of the Children’s Employment Commission, on trades and manufactures. Mines and women were the 1842 First Report. Narrowed to ‘the employment of children in factories and workshops’.
findings.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Christmas_Carol — ‘In February 1843 Dickens read the Second Report of the Children’s Employment Commission’.

findings.claim: “he laughs with genuine delight at Fezziwig’s party”.
findings.truth: Dickens says Scrooge “acted like a man out of his wits… corroborated everything, remembered everything, enjoyed everything” — no laugh. Lesson 5 and its flashcard call the Stave 5 laugh his first, and Dickens backs that with “a man who had been out of practice for so many years”. Reworded to ‘caught up with delight’.
findings.evidence: scripts/_retrofc/_texts/christmas-carol.txt Stave II, after the Fezziwig ball; Stave V “it was a splendid laugh”.

findings.claim: Flashcard 3: “What do the charwoman and laundress do at Stave 4’s opening?”
findings.truth: Old Joe’s shop is not the opening of Stave 4 — the phantom’s arrival and the businessmen’s conversation come first. Changed to ‘in Stave 4’.

findings.claim: Flashcard 1: “What are the Tiny Tim’s famous closing words?”
findings.truth: Broken wording. Corrected to ‘What are Tiny Tim’s famous closing words?’

findings.claim: Lesson 7 is titled “Structure, Language & Symbolism” but its content, description, questions and flashcards are all about themes (redemption, social responsibility, poverty, Christmas, isolation). Lesson 8 is titled “Key Themes & Exam Technique” but contains only exam technique.
findings.truth: The two titles do not match their lessons. Options: (a) swap the titles — lesson 7 becomes ‘Key Themes’, lesson 8 becomes ‘Exam Technique’; or (b) leave the titles and add the missing structure/language material to lesson 7. Recommend (a): it is a two-field change and no lesson content is wrong, only mislabelled. Title changes ripple into browse cards and the unit podcast script, so it is Tom’s call.
findings.evidence: raw/L07.txt and raw/L08.txt content vs the unit lesson list.

findings.claim: Scrooge’s reply to the charity collectors is given as one quotation: “Are there no prisons? And the Union workhouses?” (also in practice question 2).
findings.truth: In the text the gentleman answers between the two questions: “‘Are there no prisons?’ asked Scrooge… ‘And the Union workhouses?’ demanded Scrooge.” Both are Scrooge’s, so the compression is defensible; an ellipsis would be safer. Not edited.

findings.claim: Knowledge check 3 ends “keep it all the _____.’’” with a stray second closing quote mark.
findings.truth: Typographic slip only; the answer key (‘year’) is right. Not edited.

findings.claim: Lessons 5 and 7 say Scrooge “gives to the charity collectors” in Stave 5 (plural).
findings.truth: He meets one of the two portly gentlemen in the street and whispers a sum. The plural is loose shorthand, not a mark-affecting error. Not edited.

note_on_lesson_field: lesson 0 = the finding applies to all eight lessons.
summary: Every exam claim in the unit was wrong in the same three ways: 35 of 48 practice questions were labelled 20 marks, all 48 mark schemes used invented ladders (15 of them an AO1–AO4 10/10/10/10 split), and AO4 was taught as assessed in eleven places, topped by lesson 8's “worth 40 marks, split equally across AO1, AO2, AO3, and AO4” and a knowledge check keying AO4 as the accuracy objective. The board is named 18 times, twice with the spec code. On the text itself the unit is sound: every quotation checked against Gutenberg was verbatim except “Horn of Plenty” and “empty seat in the corner”, and all 40 knowledge-check keys and 8 match orders are right on the facts — the only key changed is the AO4 item, retargeted to AO3. Six content errors found: the novella does not end at Christmas dinner, “it was always said of him” is not the final line, Marley's chain does not allude to “biblical bondage”, the ‘metaphor’ pop-up defines allegory, the 1843 report was on trades not mines, and Scrooge does not laugh at Fezziwig's ball.
